problem: Every session so far has treated 'build the image' as roughly a one-time event — but a real image, once it exists, has a whole life ahead of it: new versions as code changes, new base-image patches as CVEs are disclosed (Session 117), old versions that need to eventually be deleted, and a tagging scheme that has to let you answer 'which exact image is running in production right now, and can I get back to the one before it if this deploy is broken?'

Without a deliberate image lifecycle, teams accumulate registries full of images tagged only latest, with no way to tell which build is currently deployed, no easy rollback, and no visibility into which images are safe to delete versus which are quietly still in use somewhere.
concept: Image lifecycle management is the set of practices governing an image from build through retirement:
how it's tagged and versioned, how it's promoted from dev to production, how long it's retained, and how it's eventually deprecated and deleted.

Stage What happens Build CI builds an image from a Dockerfile, tagged uniquely (commit SHA, semantic version) Scan & test Image is scanned (Session 117) and tested before promotion Push Image is pushed to a registry, tagged for its intended environment Deploy An orchestrator or host pulls the specific tag and runs it Patch/rebuild Base image updates or dependency CVEs trigger a rebuild, even with no code changes Retire Old, unused image versions are deleted from the registry on a retention policy
deep: Tags are pointers, not guarantees A tag like ethics-triage:1.0 or ethics-triage:latest is just a mutable label pointing at a specific image digest (a SHA256 hash of the image's content). Two different builds can both be tagged latest at different times — the tag moves, but nothing else. This is the single most common source of 'it worked yesterday, it's broken today' confusion in container workflows: latest is not a version, it's a moving target.
# The digest is the real, immutable identity of an image:
docker inspect --format='{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' ethics-triage:1.0 # sha256:a1b2c3... <- this never changes for this exact build # 'latest' pointing at two different digests over time:

Semantic versioning vs. commit-SHA tagging Two tagging strategies dominate in practice, and mature pipelines typically use both together: a human- readable semantic version (1.4.2) for what people talk about, and an immutable commit SHA (or build number) for what's actually deployed and traceable.

docker push registry/ethics-triage:1.4.2 docker push registry/ethics-triage:a1b2c3d docker push registry/ethics-triage:latest Layer caching across image versions Because images are built from layers (Session 114), pushing version 1.5.0 after 1.4.2 doesn't re-upload every byte — only the layers that actually changed transfer; unchanged base and dependency layers are already present in the registry and simply referenced again. This is why layer ordering discipline from Session 114 compounds in value over an image's whole lifecycle, not just its first build.
workflow: Applied as a versioning and promotion discipline for the ethics-triage image across its life:
1. Every commit to the tool's repository triggers a CI build, tagged with the commit SHA — this is the immutable, traceable artifact.
2. When that build passes tests and scanning (Session 117), it's additionally tagged with a semantic version and pushed to a 'staging' path or tag in the registry.
3. After manual or automated verification in staging, the same digest — not a rebuild — is re-tagged as production, so what's verified is exactly what deploys.
4. The previous production tag is retained, not deleted, so a rollback is just re-pointing the deployment at the prior tag rather than an emergency rebuild.

5. On a schedule (weekly or monthly), the base image is rebuilt even without code changes, to pick up security patches — this produces a new SHA and version even though the application code is identical.
6. Old, superseded versions are pruned from the registry on a retention policy (e.g. keep the last 10 production versions, delete anything older than 90 days that isn't currently deployed).
enterprise: Image lifecycle management is where container practices intersect directly with change management and release engineering — this is the layer that makes 'what's running in production' an answerable, auditable question rather than institutional memory.

Component Role CI/CD pipeline Enforces the tagging convention automatically, on every build Registry with retention policy Stores every version, prunes old ones on schedule Deployment tooling Deploys by immutable tag/digest, never by rebuilding on the fly Change management process (Layer 10, Session 145) Ties each production deployment to a specific image tag in the change record In a regulated environment like FundedNext's, this traceability isn't just operational hygiene — being able to show exactly which image (and therefore exactly which code) was running at a given point in time is often a direct compliance requirement.
dependencies: A registry that supports multiple tags per image and retains full history (Docker Hub, Google Artifact Registry, GitHub Container Registry, Amazon ECR).
A CI/CD pipeline (Layer 7, Session 111) that can apply consistent, automated tags on every build — manual tagging doesn't scale and invites human error.
Version control (Layer 7, Session 107, Git) as the source of the commit SHA that anchors every image back to exact source code.
Image scanning (Session 117) as a required gate before any tag is promoted toward production.
dependents: Rollback procedures depend entirely on retained, immutably-tagged prior versions — without them, 'rollback' becomes 'rebuild and hope it matches.'
Kubernetes deployment strategies (rolling updates, blue-green, canary — covered further in Session 119 onward) all operate on specific image tags/digests, not on 'whatever latest happens to be.'
Audit and compliance reporting depends on being able to trace a running container back to an exact, versioned image and the commit that produced it.
Disaster recovery (Layer 5, Session 80) depends on retained historical images to rebuild a known- good environment, not just retained data.
security: Risk Mitigation Deploying 'latest' directly to production Deploy by specific version tag or digest; never use a mutable tag in a production deploy command No way to trace a running container back to source code Enforce commit-SHA tagging on every CI build, non- negotiably Registry filling with stale, unscanned old images Automated retention policy; re-scan anything still deployed on a schedule Tag reused for a different image (tag mutation) Treat tags as append-only where possible; prefer deploying by digest for critical services No rollback path when a deploy goes wrong Retain the previous N production versions explicitly, never prune the currently-previous one The habit that matters most here Never deploy `latest` to anything that matters. It's convenient in a tutorial and dangerous in production, because it silently changes out from under you.
troubleshooting: Symptom Likely Cause First Command Production suddenly behaves differently with no deploy latest was pulled fresh and pointed at a new, unintended build docker inspect -- format='{{.RepoDigests}}' <image> Can't tell which code version is actually running No commit-SHA tag was ever applied Check CI logs for the build that produced the current digest Rollback attempt fails — old image not found Retention policy pruned it too aggressively Check registry retention settings; rebuild from the Git tag if truly gone Registry disk usage growing unbounded No retention/pruning policy in place List images by size/age;
implement a retention job Two team members see different 'latest' behavior Local Docker cache is stale relative to the registry docker pull explicitly rather than trusting a cached local image
example: A common real-world incident pattern: a hotfix is built and pushed as latest under time pressure, an automated deployment pulls latest and picks it up immediately in production, and the fix turns out to have a bug the tests didn't catch. Because nothing was tagged with a traceable version, the rollback target is unclear, and 'what was running an hour ago' has to be reconstructed from CI history rather than simply redeployed.

Pattern to notice The fix in this scenario isn't 'be more careful under pressure' — it's a tagging and deployment convention that makes the safe path (deploy a specific, traceable version) also the easy path, so there's nothing extra to remember during an incident.
cloud: Managed registries add lifecycle features directly on top of what plain Docker tagging provides:

Platform Lifecycle feature Google Artifact Registry Cleanup policies (auto-delete by age/count), vulnerability scanning tied to each stored version GitHub Container Registry Retention policies, and tags linked directly back to the GitHub Actions run that produced them Amazon ECR Lifecycle policies expiring untagged or old images automatically Google Cloud Run Revisions are immutable by design — every deploy creates a new, individually-addressable revision, with traffic-splitting for gradual rollout and one-command rollback Cloud Run's revision model is worth calling out specifically: it enforces good image lifecycle hygiene by default — every deployment is automatically versioned and previous revisions stay available for instant rollback, without any manual tagging discipline required.
automation: A complete CI/CD tagging and promotion flow, extending the pipeline from Session 114's automation- perspective section:
SHA=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD) docker build -t registry/ethics-triage:$SHA .
trivy image --exit-code 1 registry/ethics-triage:$SHA # Session 117 gate docker push registry/ethics-triage:$SHA # On a tagged release (e.g. git tag v1.4.2):

docker tag registry/ethics-triage:$SHA registry/ethics-triage:1.4.2 docker tag registry/ethics-triage:$SHA registry/ethics-triage:production docker push registry/ethics-triage:1.4.2 docker push registry/ethics-triage:production # Deployment tooling always pulls :production -- a controlled, # explicit promotion step, never an automatic 'latest' pull A separate, scheduled pipeline (weekly, unrelated to any code change) rebuilds from the same Dockerfile against the latest base image tag, to pick up security patches automatically — directly implementing Session 117's 'rebuild on a schedule even without code changes' guidance.
career: Image lifecycle discipline — specifically, never deploying latest and always being able to trace a running container back to exact source code — is a marker interviewers listen for when assessing whether a candidate has operated containers in a real production environment versus only in tutorials.

It also connects directly to release engineering and change management skills that matter well beyond containers specifically, since the underlying discipline (immutable, traceable, rollback-capable releases) is the same whether the artifact is a container image, a compiled binary, or a deployed script.

misconceptions: Misconception Reality 'latest' means 'the newest, best version' It's just a label — whatever was tagged latest most recently, which may not even be the newest build chronologically if tagging was manual An image only needs to be rebuilt when code changes Base image CVEs require rebuilds on a schedule Misconception Reality regardless of application code changes Tags are permanent and immutable Tags can be moved to point at a different digest at any time; only the digest itself is truly immutable Keeping every historical image version forever is 'safer' Unbounded retention just becomes registry bloat with no real traceability benefit past a reasonable window Rollback means rebuilding the old code It should mean re-deploying a retained, already-tested prior image — no rebuild needed
anchors: A tag is a sticky note on a box. The digest is what's actually inside the box. Sticky notes can be moved; contents don't change.
'latest' in production is a loaded gun pointed at your own foot — convenient in a tutorial, dangerous everywhere else.
Commit SHA tag = traceability. Semantic version tag = readability. Use both, for different audiences.
Rebuilding with no code changes isn't wasted work — it's how base-image security patches actually reach production.

lab: Hands-on: build a full tag-and-promote workflow for the ethics-triage image, including a rollback drill.

14. Build the image twice with a deliberate small change between builds (e.g. a log message), tagging each with a fake commit SHA: docker build -t ethics-triage:sha-v1 . then modify and docker build -t ethics-triage:sha-v2 ..
15. Tag sha-v1 as production: docker tag ethics-triage:sha-v1 ethics-triage:production.
16. Run the production tag and confirm its behavior.
17. Simulate a release: retag sha-v2 as production (overwriting the pointer) and run it — confirm the new behavior is now live.
18. Simulate a bad release: pretend sha-v2 has a bug. Roll back by retagging ethics-triage:sha-v1 as production again and rerunning — confirm the original behavior returns instantly, with no rebuild.

19. Inspect both images' digests with docker inspect --format='{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' (or docker images --digests locally) and confirm they're genuinely different, immutable identities regardless of what production currently points to.
20. Write out, in your own words, the retention rule you'd apply to this registry in production (e.g.
keep the last 10 tagged production versions, delete anything untagged after 30 days).

Production tie-in Step 5 is the entire value proposition of disciplined tagging: a rollback that takes seconds because the previous version was never deleted, versus an emergency rebuild under pressure.
